pct_exps.e: In a roughly normal distribution, the mean plus or minus 2 SD covers about 95% of values, which is the usual basis for a 95% reference range. One SD covers about 68% and three SD about 99.7%, so each interval answers a different question. The full observed range is distorted by extreme values and is not used for this purpose.

The USPSTF grades statin initiation strongest for adults 40 to 75 with a risk factor and 10-year risk of 10% or greater. For estimated risk of 7.5% to less than 10%, benefit is smaller, so clinicians selectively offer a statin. Patient values and preferences guide the choice. Black persons have the highest prevalence of CVD, yet the decision still follows calculated risk.
In a normal curve, mean plus or minus 1 SD covers 68.3%, 2 SD covers 95.4% and 3 SD covers 99.7% of observations. Here 2200 and 3800 are 800 g from the mean, which equals 2 SD of 400 g.

After the first hour of 0.9% saline, fluid choice depends on corrected sodium: normal or high gives 0.45% saline, low continues 0.9%. Potassium of 3.3-5.2 mEq/L is managed by adding 20-30 mEq KCl per litre to hold levels at 4.0-5.0.

Adequate future liver remnant is about 20% in a normal liver, 30% after chemotherapy, and 40% in cirrhosis. If inadequate, portal vein embolization diverts flow to the remnant causing hypertrophy over weeks. ALPPS is an alternative.

Safe resection requires a future liver remnant of about 20% in a normal liver, 30% after chemotherapy, and 40% in cirrhosis. If inadequate, portal vein embolisation diverts flow to the remnant, causing hypertrophy over 4 to 6 weeks. ALPPS is an alternative.

About 85% of children seroconvert at 9 months, rising to over 95% at 12 months, because of maternal antibody interference. This primary vaccine failure is why a second dose is given, to cover non-responders and build herd immunity of about 95%.

SJS involves under 10% detachment, overlap 10 to 30%, and TEN over 30% body surface area. Common triggers are anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and nevirapine. Management includes stopping the drug and supportive care.

The NASCET and ECST methods measure carotid stenosis differently, so reports must state which criteria were used. For symptomatic stenosis of 50% to 99% by NASCET, urgent endarterectomy referral is advised alongside best medical treatment. Stenosis below 50% by NASCET gets best medical treatment alone.

Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% to 99% by NASCET criteria carries a high early stroke risk, so surgery is offered promptly. Stable patients fit for surgery are referred urgently to a service meeting national standards. Best medical treatment, including antiplatelets, statins and blood pressure control, continues alongside surgery. Stenosis below 50% by NASCET does not benefit from surgery.

NICE sets a 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) target for diet alone or medicines without hypoglycaemia risk, and 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) for hypoglycaemia-associated medicines. The 58 mmol/mol (7.5%) figure is a trigger to intensify treatment rather than a target. Targets should be individualised and agreed with the person.

NICE sets individual HbA1c targets for adults with type 2 diabetes, with the level depending on the medicines used. Targets are 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) for lifestyle or non-hypoglycaemic regimens and 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) for medicines linked to hypoglycaemia. If HbA1c rises to 58 mmol/mol (7.5%) or higher on the initial regimen, reinforce lifestyle advice and intensify treatment.

SJS and TEN lie on a continuum of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, usually drug induced, with epidermal necrosis and mucosal involvement. Detachment under 10% of body surface area defines SJS, 10 to 30% defines overlap, and over 30% defines TEN. A positive Nikolsky sign supports the diagnosis. Early specialist input is essential.

Symptomatic carotid stenosis is classified using NASCET or ECST criteria, and reports must state which was used. Symptomatic NASCET stenosis of 50% to 99% is referred urgently for endarterectomy. Best medical treatment, including antiplatelets and cholesterol lowering, continues alongside. Stenosis below 50% by NASCET is managed medically without surgery.

A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value (a ratio of 1 for ratio measures) corresponds to a non-significant result at the 5% level. Crucially, the interval also shows the range of effects compatible with the data. Here the data are compatible with anything from a small reduction to a 33% increase, so the study is inconclusive rather than reassuring.

ESC categorises heart failure by LVEF: HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41% to 49%, HFpEF 50% or more. HFpEF additionally needs elevated natriuretic peptides (NT-proBNP 125 pg/mL or more, or BNP 35 pg/mL or more) plus structural or diastolic abnormality.

ESC classifies heart failure by LVEF: HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41% to 49%, HFpEF 50% or more. HFpEF additionally needs elevated natriuretic peptides (NT-proBNP 125 pg/mL or more or BNP 35 pg/mL or more) with structural or diastolic dysfunction.

Canadian Diabetes Association criteria use HbA1c to classify glycemia: 6.0% to 6.4% indicates prediabetes and 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes when confirmed. Fasting glucose of 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L is impaired fasting glucose, a separate category. Any abnormal test in these ranges should be interpreted alongside the others. Screening adults with risk factors such as obesity and South Asian ancestry supports earlier testing.

Total body water is about 60% of body weight in an adult man, split roughly two-thirds intracellular and one-third extracellular. The extracellular third includes plasma, about 5% of body weight, and interstitial fluid. Free water from 5% dextrose distributes across all body water, so the intracellular compartment receives the largest share once glucose is metabolised. Adipose tissue holds little water; after glucose is metabolised the infusion is free water shared by body-water fractions, mostly intracellular.

Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and specificity. In 1000 people with 10% prevalence, 90% sensitivity gives 90 true positives. Specificity of 80% leaves 180 false positives among 900 healthy people. Thus only one in three positives is true, so confirmatory testing is needed.

The image shows an endocranial (cerebral) view of a dry left temporal bone. The thin, flat, shell-like plate above is the squamous part, with shallow impressions from the temporal lobe (cerebral markings). The dense, wedge or pyramid-shaped ridge running obliquely forward and medially across the lower part of the specimen is the petrous part. It carries an oval opening on its posterior surface, consistent with the internal acoustic meatus (transmitting CN VII, CN VIII and the labyrinthine vessels). The petrous part is the hardest bone in the body and houses the middle and inner ear structures: cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals, facial canal, and carotid canal. It separates the middle from the posterior cranial fossa. Fractures through it are classified as longitudinal (about 70-90%, parallel to the long axis, with ossicular injury, conductive hearing loss, and CN VII palsy in about 20%) or transverse (about 10-30%, perpendicular to the long axis, with sensorineural hearing loss, and CN VII palsy in about 50%). Clinical signs of a skull base fracture include Battle sign, hemotympanum, CSF otorrhea and cranial nerve deficits.

LCIS is a risk marker for subsequent invasive breast cancer in either breast (roughly 1% per year in older series, with lifetime risk in the range of 20% to 30%), but it is not an invasive cancer and does not require excision or axillary surgery. When LCIS is incidental, concordant, and fully evaluated with no additional lesion, management is surveillance and discussion of risk reduction. Chemoprevention with tamoxifen or raloxifene (premenopausal and postmenopausal) or an aromatase inhibitor (postmenopausal) reduces risk. Option A is wrong because re-excision is indicated for atypical lesions or discordance, not for LCIS alone, since the lesion is not a precursor requiring clear margins. Option B is wrong because bilateral mastectomy is disproportionate for LCIS alone; it is considered only in select high-risk patients after shared decision-making. Option D is wrong because axillary surgery has no role when there is no invasive carcinoma.

The widely used thresholds (Vauthey and colleagues; Schwartz and Sabiston HPB chapters) are about 20% FLR for normal liver, about 30% after prolonged chemotherapy (steatohepatitis or sinusoidal injury), and about 40% for cirrhosis or after significant chemotherapy with sinusoidal injury. This patient has cirrhosis plus chemotherapy-associated injury, so 40% is the appropriate threshold. The correct answer is C. If the FLR is inadequate, portal vein embolization (PVE), or staged approaches such as ALPPS or liver venous deprivation, are used to induce hypertrophy. Option A is wrong because the 20% figure applies only to healthy parenchyma, and this patient is cirrhotic with sinusoidal injury. Option B is wrong because 30% is inadequate for a cirrhotic liver, and extra chemotherapy worsens sinusoidal injury. Option D is wrong because the 50% figure is not the standard threshold, and pump placement does nothing to increase remnant volume.

Correct answer: right portal vein embolization (PVE). In cirrhotic liver, the generally accepted safe FLR threshold is about 40% of standard liver volume, versus about 20% in a healthy liver and about 30% after chemotherapy. This patient's FLR of 28% is below the cirrhosis threshold, so resection carries unacceptable risk of post-hepatectomy liver failure. PVE induces hypertrophy of the contralateral (left) lobe and is the standard way to increase FLR before extended resection. Direct resection is unsafe at this FLR. Left hepatectomy alone would not remove the tumor in segments 5 to 8 and so is not oncologically appropriate. Sorafenib is not a substitute for resection in a resectable tumor and does not reliably increase FLR.

Correct: CEA within 14 days (ideally within 2 weeks) of a symptomatic stenosis of 50-99% is the guideline standard (ESVS 2023, SVS, ACST-1/NASCET pooled analysis). Early intervention reduces the high early recurrent stroke risk, which is greatest in the first 2 weeks. Distractor A: deferring surgery for 6 months forfeits the period of highest stroke risk; antiplatelet therapy is adjunctive, not a substitute. Distractor C: elective stenting after 6 weeks is too late for a symptomatic lesion and ignores the timing benefit; CREST and ICSS show CEA and CAS are comparable in stroke risk in most patients, but the timing of intervention, not the modality, is what matters here. Distractor D: medical therapy alone is inadequate for a symptomatic 75% lesion; the 80% threshold applies to asymptomatic disease, and NASCET showed benefit from CEA at 70% or greater.

Chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) is defined as a sustained decline in FEV1 of 20% or more from the post-transplant baseline, confirmed on repeat testing, after other causes have been excluded. Here the fall is from 2.8 L to 2.1 L, a decline of 25%, which meets the threshold for BOS, the most common CLAD phenotype. Option A is wrong because the threshold for CLAD is a 20% decline, not 30%. Option C is wrong because the FEV1 is not below 1.0 L, and grading depends on the degree of decline. Option D is wrong because the picture fits CLAD and is not explained by acute cellular rejection, which typically causes a reversible drop in lung function.

Correct answer: B. In symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50 to 99% (NASCET, ESVS, and SVS guidelines), carotid endarterectomy provides absolute benefit that is greatest when performed within about 2 weeks of the ipsilateral event, when stroke recurrence risk is highest. Surgery should be done by a team with perioperative stroke and death rates below 6%. Distractor A ignores the proven benefit of revascularisation for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis and fails to address the early high-risk window. Distractor C is inappropriate because stenting is generally reserved for high surgical risk, anatomically unfavourable lesions, or restenosis after CEA; the 6-month delay also forfeits the early benefit. Distractor D is wrong because surveillance alone is for asymptomatic stenosis, and waiting 12 months leaves the patient exposed to recurrent stroke.

In biliary atresia, the age at which Kasai portoenterostomy is performed is the single most critical determinant of native liver survival and restoration of bile flow. Surgery performed before 60 days of life results in bile drainage restoration rates of 70-80%, dropping to 40-50% between 60-90 days, and < 20% after 90 days due to irreversible progressive portal tract fibrosis and obliteration of microscopic biliary ductules at the porta hepatis.

In pediatric LDLT for infants and small children (< 10-15 kg), the left lateral segment (Segments II and III) is the standard graft of choice. The optimal graft-to-recipient weight ratio (GRWR) is 1.0% to 3.0% (or 4.0%). A GRWR > 4.0% leads to 'large-for-size' syndrome: abdominal compartment syndrome, compression of the graft, kinking of the hepatic vein and portal vein, hypoperfusion, and poor graft survival. If the left lateral segment is too large (>4%), monosegment (Segment II or III) or reduced-size grafting is performed.

In pediatric ALL, Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) measured at the end of induction (Day 29/33) is the single most powerful prognostic factor for relapse across all protocols. An MRD threshold of < 0.01% (< 10^-4, or 1 blast in 10,000 cells) defines MRD negativity and favorable outcome. An end-induction MRD >= 0.01% (such as 0.15% in this patient) denotes high risk of relapse and mandates post-induction chemotherapy intensification (escalation to high-risk blocks or consideration of immunotherapy/transplant if persistently positive).

ordinary_exps.e: Physicians with suspected substance use impairment must be removed promptly from clinical duties, because judgment and motor skills may be compromised. Referral to a physician health program offers confidential evaluation, monitoring, and treatment, with structured return-to-work agreements when appropriate. Colleagues also have an ethical and often legal duty to report concerns.

Quality improvement uses rapid, iterative plan-do-study-act cycles to test changes on a small scale. Root cause review here identifies undocumented indications and delayed removal as drivers. Small tests allow learning before successful interventions are spread.

Surrogates decide by substituted judgment, reconstructing the patient's own wishes, and a valid advance directive written while competent is the best evidence of those wishes. When a surrogate's views conflict with a clear directive, clinicians should review the document, clarify the patient's values with the agent, and seek ethics consultation rather than defaulting to either side. Court involvement is reserved for disputes that remain unresolved.

Disclosure of medical errors that cause harm is an ethical duty and an expectation in US practice. Clinicians should explain what happened, acknowledge the error, apologize, and describe steps to prevent recurrence. Internal safety reporting feeds quality improvement, while honest communication preserves trust with patients and families.

When a patient lacks capacity and has no advance directive, a surrogate is chosen under state law, usually a spouse first. The surrogate uses substituted judgment, based on what the patient would want, or best interests if that is unknown. Ethics consultation helps resolve family conflict.

Decision-making capacity is decision-specific and requires understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and a consistent choice. Accurate restatement of information shows understanding but does not by itself establish appreciation, which mania or psychosis may impair. Surrogate decisions or implied consent are used only after capacity is found lacking.

Minors in most states can consent to care for sexually transmitted infections, pregnancy testing, and contraception without parental permission. Confidentiality encourages adolescents to seek testing and treatment. Clinicians should explain the exceptions to confidentiality, such as risk of serious harm or abuse, before the visit.

Disclosure of harmful medical errors is an ethical and professional duty. Clinicians should promptly tell the patient what happened, apologize, explain consequences and describe corrective actions. Institutional reporting and root cause analysis proceed in parallel, not in place of disclosure.

Impairment from substance use or mental illness is a patient-safety issue, and clinicians have ethical and often legal duties to act on reasonable concern. Immediate removal from patient care, followed by formal evaluation through a physician health program, is the standard approach. Recovery-oriented programs support treatment and a safe return to practice when appropriate.

In most US jurisdictions, minors can consent to contraception, pregnancy-related care, and STI testing and treatment without parental permission. AAP guidance supports confidential adolescent interviews and limits disclosure to parents to situations required by law or involving serious safety risk. Clinicians should explain the limits of confidentiality at the start of the visit.

Most US states allow minors to consent to confidential evaluation and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, contraception, and substance use. Clinicians should interview adolescents alone for part of the visit, explain exceptions to confidentiality such as abuse or serious risk of harm, and then order testing. Confidentiality supports honest history-taking and prompt care.

When a patient lacks capacity and has no designated proxy, US states use default surrogate hierarchies, often placing adult children as a class. Surrogates apply substituted judgment, deciding as the patient would, using prior statements and values. Disagreement among surrogates should prompt family meetings and, if unresolved, an ethics consultation.

Impaired physicians pose a serious patient safety risk and need immediate removal from clinical duties. Confidential evaluation through a physician health program supports diagnosis and treatment. Colleagues have an ethical duty to act and may report under institutional and state rules.

Disclosure of a medical error is an ethical and professional obligation, and US institutions expect prompt, honest communication with apology. The patient should receive a factual explanation of what happened, its expected effects, and the monitoring plan. Internal event reporting supports root cause analysis and system improvement rather than blame.

Surrogate decisions should apply substituted judgment, reflecting what the patient would want based on known values, and the spouse typically holds priority in the surrogate hierarchy. Family conflict and uncertain values warrant ethics consultation and a structured family meeting. Continuing or withdrawing treatment should follow this deliberation, not a unilateral decision.

Physician impairment from substance use or illness threatens patient safety and requires immediate removal from clinical duties. Confidential physician health programs assess, treat, and monitor clinicians, and many states require reporting of impaired practitioners. The response is supportive but protective of patients.

A capable adult may refuse any treatment, including blood transfusion, even when death is a likely outcome. Advance directives and informed refusal are respected when the patient has capacity at the time of the decision. Surrogates decide only when the patient lacks capacity, and emergency exceptions do not override a known, valid refusal.

Minors generally can consent to contraception, STI testing and treatment in the US. Confidential care encourages adolescents to seek preventive and treatment services. Clinicians should explain the limits of confidentiality at the outset, such as concerns about abuse or serious risk of harm.

Physicians with suspected impairment, from substance use, psychiatric illness or neurologic disease, pose patient-safety risks that require prompt action. Many state physician health programs offer confidential assessment and monitoring, and workplace leaders have a duty to act on credible reports. Impairment is a medical condition as well as a professional matter, and protective steps do not require proof before they begin.

Surrogates for incapacitated patients apply substituted judgment, based on prior expressed wishes, or best interest when wishes are unknown. Most states place a spouse high in the surrogate hierarchy, but family conflict signals the need for structured meetings. Ethics consultation and palliative care help resolve disagreement before any withdrawal.

Honest disclosure of adverse events, including an apology and a description of corrective steps, is a core professional and ethical duty in US practice. Disclosure should be prompt and factual, and institutional review proceeds in parallel rather than replacing physician communication. Physicians should not speculate about causes before the review is complete.

Decision-making capacity is decision-specific and depends on understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a consistent choice, not on speech. Patients with ALS may communicate with eye blinks, eye gaze, or assistive devices. A capable patient may refuse life-sustaining treatment, and this refusal takes precedence over family preferences, with palliative care supporting comfort.

VACTERL is an association rather than a syndrome, with no single known cause, and recurrence is generally low. Because the clustering is not explained by one gene, counselling focuses on reassurance and appropriate prenatal assessment rather than reproductive restriction. Unexpected intellectual disability should prompt reconsideration of a specific syndrome.

Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia presents in the newborn with choking, drooling, and failure to pass a feeding tube, which is a surgical emergency. Oral feeds risk aspiration through the fistula. Initial care is airway protection, head elevation, continuous suction of the upper pouch, and urgent pediatric surgical referral, while cardiac and renal imaging can follow.

VACTERL is an association: its components cluster more often than chance but have no single known cause. Most cases are sporadic, and no single gene explains most of them. Counseling should convey a generally low recurrence risk and arrange genetic review to exclude definable syndromes.

VACTERL is a non-random association diagnosed clinically when at least three component features are present without an alternative unifying syndrome. Here four components are present, and normal chromosome breakage studies argue against Fanconi anemia. Normal intellect fits the association rather than a syndrome with intellectual disability.

VACTERL is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, and intellect is usually normal in affected children. Marked developmental delay or dysmorphism should prompt reconsideration of a specific syndrome. Targeted genetic testing and chromosomal microarray can reveal an alternative unifying diagnosis, such as a deletion syndrome.

Lung LDCT screening applies to adults 50 to 80 years with a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. Eligibility uses both pack-years and time since quitting, so large past exposure does not qualify a former smoker who quit long ago. Screening stops after 15 years without smoking or when a health problem limits life expectancy or surgical candidacy. Shared decision-making should precede any screening.

The USPSTF recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years. For women with dense breasts and a negative mammogram, the evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of supplemental ultrasound or MRI. Clinicians should therefore continue standard screening and discuss this uncertainty.

USPSTF recommends annual low-dose CT for adults aged 50 to 80 years with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years. Age is a required criterion, so a 49-year-old is not yet eligible despite heavy smoking. Every current smoker should receive cessation interventions regardless of screening eligibility.
